item.title: LibreOffice was downloaded 9.4 million times over the last 8 weeks, with 2026's stats already beating 2025
item.itunes:title: LibreOffice was downloaded 9.4 million times over the last 8 weeks, with 2026's stats already beating 2025
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • LibreOffice hit 9.4M downloads in eight weeks, a notable surge from under 1M/week.
  • Possible drivers: Publisher's end, Europe's push for digital sovereignty, and v26.8 features.
  • 2026 downloads already surpass 2025 with ten weeks left—momentum could carry into 2027.

Did you grab LibreOffice over the last eight weeks? If so, you helped The Document Foundation with a huge milestone. The foundation reported that it got 9.4 million downloads over an eight-week period, and 2026's stats already beat 2025.

LibreOffice enjoyed 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks

It's already breaking records

As announced on the LibreOffice blog, the Foundation checked how many times the productivity suite was downloaded between August 24th and October 18th. Beforehand, it was getting under 1 million downloads a week, so 9.4 million in eight weeks shows a notable improvement.

So, what caused this influx of downloads? Unfortunately, as is always the case with software downloads, there's no little questionnaire people filled out to tell us why. My personal take is a combination of the following:

  • Microsoft recently pulled the plug on Publisher, with LibreOffice advertising that it could pick up the slack.
  • Europe took more steps toward digital sovereignty, which may have inspired more people to embrace open-source products.
  • LibreOffice 26.8 was released back in August, which included support for Microsoft Office features and a fresh "no AI features" statement.

The Document Foundation isn't so sure, either, but they believe it's because their product is working well:

We like to think that the consistency of the LibreOffice project – which has been championing the concept of digital sovereignty and standard document formats for years – and the robustness of the software, which has never sought to be a clone of the most widely used office suite on the market but has always strived to forge its own path, are two very important factors that, in the long term, represent a significant advantage over all other products.

The cool part is that LibreOffice has already seen more downloads in 2026 than in 2025, and we're still ten weeks from the turn of the year. Here's hoping 2027 will do the same.

LibreOffice 26.8's release fixes your word spacing, brings in a new Notebookbar UI, and still contains zero AI

Sometimes, less is more.

1
By  Simon Batt

item.title: 4 things I'd do with a cheap used thin client before buying a new mini PC
item.itunes:title: 4 things I'd do with a cheap used thin client before buying a new mini PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A thin client is the least exciting device for a normal user. It's something you only see in college and school labs, or workplaces that need a just-enough usable computer to run a bunch of software. In contrast, a mini PC feels more exciting because it has a fairly diverse use case. You can pick entry-level devices with Intel N100 and N150 chips, or go with something more powerful like a six/eight-core CPU and a discrete GPU. For home servers or just as an additional computer, the entry-level mini PCs are more suitable.

I wanted to buy a mini PC, but in these testing times, even devices that used to be cheap retail at mind-boggling prices. So, I spotted a used thin client and gave it a try after a quick memory and storage upgrade. There's adequate power hiding inside the bland exterior, and here are four ways I would repurpose it.

Use it as a spare computer

Several Linux distributions can help

If you have a thin client that once used to run Windows 10 and cannot run the next one, it's still useful as a spare computer. Linux distributions like AntiX can revive old thin clients and offer a very lightweight design. Similarly, MX Linux Fluxbox is another lightweight distribution that doesn't even have a desktop environment. It aims to provide a desktop-like experience through a window manager. These distributions can run on under 500MB of memory and don't need much GPU power.

5 operating systems for reviving your old PC as a server

Even a dinosaur PC can be resurrected as a home lab

8
By  Ayush Pande

You can install browsers and a few other tools like LibreOffice to build a basic PC suite. A spare computer doesn't need much, and as long as it can play media and surf the web, anyone in your family can use it. Another idea is to use it as a learning computer for Linux and programming. Use a purely CLI OS like Ubuntu Server to slowly learn the ropes and master the terminal and OS basics.

Build a local cloud storage

Ditch Google and Microsoft’s duopoly

Building a local cloud storage is actually one of the simplest things you can do with a thin client. You can install a lean x86 OS like Ubuntu Server or DietPi and then install Nextcloud. You can also deploy it as a Docker container and run Immich alongside it. I recommend the latter, since containerization is better than installing packages individually. Even if you hate Nextcloud's apps for documents, sheets, and meetings, the basic file sync feature is enough to convince you.

Once you have the server set up, you can install Nextcloud client apps on your phone and PC. After a quick file mapping and sync job, the tool will automatically create backups on the server. Most thin clients support SATA HDDs and SSDs, and you can add an extra drive and use it only for Nextcloud backups. A thin client also has multiple external ports for connectivity, and even USB-to-SATA enclosures will work fine.

9 Docker containers that run 24/7 on my $100 mini PC

Maximum value budget homelab.

18
By  Samir Makwana

I mentioned Immich because it's a great alternative to Google Photos. Nextcloud has basic image backup and preview, but Immich takes it to the next level. It supports OCR and can use machine learning to improve file mapping and search. A thin client might not be able to handle the machine learning features of the tool, but you can still connect your Nextcloud library to it.

Host a suite of lightweight apps

Several things to save money on

Lately, I've been curious about lightweight, self-hosted tools that can replace paid subscriptions. While I host Vaultwarden on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, I can also host it on the HP t620 thin client I got a few weeks back. The password manager is fully capable of replacing both Chrome and paid tools. I was a devoted LastPass user for years before finally switching to Vaultwarden.

Since a password manager should have 24/7 uptime, you'll need uninterrupted power and network connectivity. You'll also need Tailscale Serve or a reverse proxy to enable HTTPS. The next thing you can host is a PDF editor like BentoPDF or Stirling PDF. BentoPDF is a lightweight implementation and surprisingly good for such a small tool. Stirling PDF is more demanding, but the features are also comparable to paid tools like Adobe Acrobat. A thin client won't have problems running either of them.

I squeezed DietPi onto a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and it replaced my $50-a-month cloud setup

DietPi’s lean footprint unlocks a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W that hosts secure backups, ad filtering and browser tools.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Another lightweight app you can host is OmniTools. It's a purely client-side processing app like BentoPDF and runs on even the weakest SBCs without stutters. Your thin client can run it without issues. Beyond this trio, you can host a local download client for large, uninterrupted downloads.

Network-wide ad blocker and DNS resolver

Pi-hole, Unbound, or any other tool

It's possible to squeeze the Pi-hole and Unbound combo on a puny Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It'll serve as a network-wide ad blocker while Unbound acts as a private DNS resolver. You could use Cloudflare or another DNS provider, but since self-hosting is about maximum privacy, this basic combo gives you the best of both worlds. AdGuard is another tool to block website tracking and remove ads. But it's a more demanding service and needs a powerful SBC or a mini PC.

Why I moved Pi-hole from my NAS to a dedicated Raspberry Pi, and why you should too

From fragile dependency to rock-solid reliability: The story of moving a critical service to a dedicated device.

29
By  Jeff Butts

Another idea is to build a primary DNS resolver and sinkhole on the thin client, using the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W and an alternate one. So, if one goes down, your internet access won't be cut off. Thin clients also have built-in Ethernet ports, which is a perk for a stable connection compared to Wi-Fi.

Old but still useful

A thin client deserves more praise than it gets. Earlier, I saw SBCs as the cheapest option for a home server use case, but thin clients match that price with better performance. An old thin client is still cheaper than a new mini-PC, and less powerful. But you can run most self-hosted tools without worry, and you can upgrade memory and storage.

item.title: Logitech's MK955 Signature Slim keyboard combo drops to its lowest price of 2026
item.itunes:title: Logitech's MK955 Signature Slim keyboard combo drops to its lowest price of 2026
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've been eyeing the Logitech Signature Slim MK955 keyboard combo, now is a prime time to pull the trigger. The set has dropped to its lowest price of the year at $100 on Amazon, a reasonable drop from the $120 retail price.

Logitech Signature Slim MK955 keyboard combo
See at Amazon

It's going to elevate your typing experience

Credit: Logitech

The typing experience is defined by Logitech's low-profile scissor keys. They offer a laptop-like feel with a 10-key number pad for those who live in spreadsheets. The included mouse is equally thoughtful, featuring Silent Touch technology that reduces click noise by 90% compared to standard mice.

This is a game-changer for open-plan offices or late-night work sessions where you don't want to disturb anyone. It also supports Easy-Switch technology, allowing you to connect to up to three devices simultaneously and toggle between them with a single button press. This is invaluable for anyone juggling a work laptop, a personal desktop, and a tablet.

Battery life is another area where this set shines. The keyboard runs on two AAA batteries and is rated for up to three years of use. The mouse takes a single AA battery and lasts up to two years. With Logi Bolt wireless technology providing a stable connection up to 10 meters away, you can keep your desk clutter-free without worrying about signal dropouts.

At $100, the value proposition is hard to ignore. You're getting a durable, comfortable keyboard-and-mouse combo with exceptional battery life. If you need a reliable keyboard and mouse that just works, this deal is worth grabbing before it runs out of stock.

item.title: Claude's new rich text editor replaced Google Docs for me, and it already knows my entire project before I type anything
item.itunes:title: Claude's new rich text editor replaced Google Docs for me, and it already knows my entire project before I type anything
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most AI-generated files end up living somewhere completely different from where they were created. A chatbot can draft your task list or spec sheet, then you put it in a Google Doc, owned by a completely different company. Wherever you put the notes, that doc ends up with no idea about the conversation behind it. Then Anthropic launched its own editor inside Claude in September, which completely cuts out the middleman between AI synthesis and note-taking. I've been using it in regular chats and in Claude Code, and I think it might have started replacing Google Docs for me.

I integrated Google Drive into Claude and my productivity tripled in no time

Beyond copy-paste

By  Parth Shah

What is Claude Docs?

It's not Google Docs wearing a Claude badge

Claude Docs is Anthropic's own rich-text editor, which launched alongside Claude Slides in September, and it isn't a Google product in any form. It actually confused me a bit at first because I'm so used to associating the word "Doc" with Google Docs, and there are also multiple things sharing the same name in Claude right now: Anthropic's developer documentation, the connector that edits your actual Google Docs, and Claude Docs.

A doc lives in your Claude account, and whatever you make will end up in the Artifacts tab, so you can get back to that doc from any conversation. Claude Docs is available on all the tiers, including Free, and it's also switched on by default. An important distinction is that Claude Docs is separate from the file creation that Claude has had for ages. For example, a .docx that Claude generates is finished once you download it. But a Claude Doc stays open and editable by both you and Claude.

There are a couple of surfaces where you'll encounter docs in Claude. Firstly, you've probably noticed lately that responses in the chatbot end with a "Create Doc" option at the bottom. You can also ask the chat at any point to make a doc, or just type the /doc command if you don't want Claude to guess what you want. When opened to full view, the doc gets its own menu where you can pop it out into a separate window or open it in your browser, plus you can split one into tabs like sections of a notebook. And as I've mentioned, they also live in Artifacts - so you can go straight to the Artifacts tab and create one from scratch.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Everything I used in Google Docs is also in Claude Docs

It covers pretty much everything, and more

The first time I asked for a doc, Claude didn't just hand me a finished page. It put up an outline and then filled in the sections one at a time while I could watch it live, and since it's not locked while it's at work, I could also type into the doc alongside it. Hitting the slash brings up the block menu with all your usuals like headers and list options, and you've got a couple more formatting tools in the top toolbar such as tables and image inserts.

The comments are what make it worth even creating a doc. You highlight anything in the doc and tag @claude, add your commentary or ask Claude a question or for revisions. It will respond in that thread once it's made the edit, with a short note on what's changed. There are quick buttons for making sections shorter or simpler as well. The thing is, Claude responds to all of these little interactions with the full context of the session in mind. So you're not just slapping AI on top of the notes, you're interacting with the entire chat in an organized fashion, basically.

At first I didn't realize it had version history, but, similar to Google Docs, it's tucked away in the top-left dropdown; this will show you a list of all the edits. Then there's also export. You can get out your document as a Word file, PDF, Markdown file, or send it straight to Google Docs or Notion. This is ultimately what makes Claude Docs a true Google Docs replacement because you can slot this into pretty much any workflow with any tool stack.

The one area it trails behind is sharing. Whoever opens your link needs a Claude account, and there's no comment-only role for people who should only leave notes. I'd also be careful with deleting, since there's no trash to pull a doc back out of.

4 unique ways I use Claude that has nothing to do with coding

The Claude revolution.

By  Parth Shah

It already knows your projects before you type anything

All it needs is a sentence and a folder

Docs in regular chat can already draw on your files and memory, plus whatever apps you've connected, but Claude Code is where this gets super useful. A Claude Code session already sits inside a folder, so when you ask for a doc it reads the actual files instead of working off whatever you've said in the chat. Plus it knows everything that's happened in that session.

Here, I opened a session in a copy of my Obsidian vault and typed one sentence asking for a status brief, with a table of what's active and what's stalled, without pasting in any notes. It built an empty skeleton first, with placeholders where each section would go, and asked permission before editing the doc. Then it read through my files and filled everything in.

My vault has dashboards that are supposed to track all of this, and Claude noticed they hadn't been regenerated in a hot minute, so it just ignored them and sorted things by each file's real last-edited date instead. The status column used little colored labels you can click to change, like Active or Stalled, instead of plain text. Further down, the next steps were a checklist I could actually tick off.

A blank Google Doc would've left me digging through the vault myself to fill in that table. Here the doc already knew the whole project before I typed anything.

I turned Claude into my productivity command center with these tools

Claude gets better with the right tools.

2
By  Parth Shah

Starting from context instead of nothing

Google Docs isn't disappearing for me entirely, mainly because other people still send me links to projects and briefs. It also has Gemini which can handle comments and it can dig through my Drive, but turning a proper Gemini conversation into a doc still means building it in the Gemini app and exporting it over. This is why I keep starting in Claude Docs now instead, everything is properly integrated.

item.title: Emulators save games that publishers have abandoned, but the industry still treats them like piracy
item.itunes:title: Emulators save games that publishers have abandoned, but the industry still treats them like piracy
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Game preservation has an uncomfortable problem. Many of the games worth saving are the hardest to access. Either publishers stopped selling them years ago, or the original console is too hard to maintain. With digital storefronts shutting down and games getting delisted on a whim, emulation often remains the most practical way to keep old titles alive.

However, emulation also falls into a legal grey area due to the obvious question over ROM acquisition and cracked encryption. Emulators give users the digital infrastructure to play old titles, but game ownership is often up in the air. Publishers have fought tooth and nail to protect their IP, sometimes going too far and shutting down small-time emulation projects that can't afford protracted legal battles.

Emulators aren't the only way to preserve obscure titles — FPGAs and decompilation have picked up pace — but it remains one of the most accessible. How legitimate preservation efforts make their presence felt will determine the future of emulation.

For thousands of titles, emulation remains the only way to play

Gamers don't realize what they would have lost

Emulating is often the only lifeboat lesser-known titles have. Although emulating popular titles gets the most attention, the obscure ones on the fringes arguably need the technology most. Older consoles can get nearly impossible to maintain after a point, publishers can go out of business and take their library with them, or the game can become otherwise impossible to purchase due to licensing or storefront availability issues.

Preservationists, enthusiasts, and researchers want to keep older games alive for as long as possible since they form a crucial part of gaming history. A 2023 study by the Video Game History Foundation showed that 87% of classic games were no longer commercially available. Emulation is sometimes the only way to keep these titles from disappearing completely.

Projects like MAME have effectively saved thousands of classic games from the 70s, 80s, and 90s coin-op arcade history. MAME mimics the physical microchips, sound boards, and visual layouts of thousands of systems to preserve classic titles as authentically as possible. Then, there's RetroArch, which centralized game preservation efforts by integrating dozens of console platforms, from the Atari 2600 to the PlayStation 2, into a single front-end.

Games like The Outfoxies and Golden Axe: The Revenge of Death Adder were never ported to home consoles, so emulators like MAME and Finding Burn Neo were the only way to play them. ScummVM brought iconic titles like Blade Runner, The MADS collection, and The Feeble Files back from digital obsolescence when the original source code was lost, storefronts completely dropped the titles, or the game engine was broken on modern Windows architecture.

Fans of classic games and gamers, in general, have a lot to thank these projects for. Many of them continue to maintain tens of thousands of titles spanning dozens of console systems. That said, the road to game preservation has never been smooth.

4 best operating systems you should consider for retro gaming emulation

There are many options to choose from

1
By  Anurag Singh

Publishers are ruthless when going after emulation

Emulation is often lumped together with piracy

  • Credit: Nintendo
  • Credit: Nintendo

Emulation isn't inherently illegal, as evidenced by numerous legal verdicts in favor of the technology. As long as the emulator doesn't use copyrighted parts of the original console's OS, the project is in the clear. Most emulators are developed without accessing the console's source code, a practice known as clean-room design; therefore, these projects are protected under "fair use."

item.title: I thought self-hosting would save me money, but my years of experience proved otherwise
item.itunes:title: I thought self-hosting would save me money, but my years of experience proved otherwise
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
At first, I saw self-hosting as a simple way to cut my monthly expenses. Why pay for software when I could run free, open-source alternatives on my own hardware? It seemed like an easy decision, especially when I wanted more control over my data and the tools I used. But after years of self-hosting, I realized the financial side wasn't as straightforward as I expected. The more I explored, the more I questioned whether I was actually saving money. Here's what changed my perspective and how I approach self-hosting today.

The software was free, but nothing else was

Free software comes with a price

Most of the tools I wanted to self-host were open-source, and I could run them on my own hardware without paying for licenses. On paper, it looked like an easy way to cut recurring expenses.

But the software was only one part of the equation. I also had to account for electricity to keep my services running around the clock, extra storage for my growing file collection, and external drives to keep backups safe. Networking equipment and replacement drives added to the expenses, too.

These costs were easy to ignore because they rarely showed up together. But over time, these small expenses added up. I was avoiding monthly subscriptions, yet self-hosting was costing me more than the price of the software suggested.

My time became the most expensive part

The hidden cost of constant maintenance

The highest cost I underestimated was the time I spent keeping everything running. Setting up a self-hosted service is usually straightforward, but keeping it running smoothly is a different story. I often found myself troubleshooting failed updates, checking logs, fixing configuration issues, and figuring out why something that worked yesterday had suddenly stopped working.

Even small problems could take longer than expected. Sometimes, I would sit down to use a service only to spend the next hour fixing it instead. I also had to keep track of updates and make sure changes didn't break other parts of my setup.

I enjoy experimenting with technology, but maintaining services can quickly turn that excitement into a chore. My time has value, too, and spending an entire evening fixing a minor issue isn't always worth it. The more services I hosted, the more time I needed to keep everything running.

After years of self-hosting, here are 5 mistakes I will never make again

These hard-earned lessons completely changed how I approach self-hosting.

By  Yash Patel

Not every service is worth self-hosting

Convenience has a price, and I started missing it

Over time, I stopped treating every subscription as something I needed to replace. Just because I could self-host an alternative didn't mean it was the smarter choice. Some services were inexpensive enough that running my own version offered very little financial benefit. Others required too much effort for something I barely used.

I started looking at what I was actually getting from a paid service. If a subscription cost only a few dollars a month and worked reliably across all my devices, replacing it wasn't always worth the effort. I also had to consider features that open-source alternatives might lack or require extra configuration to match.

Now, I choose what to self-host more carefully. I prefer running services that offer meaningful privacy, control, or long-term savings. For everything else, I'm comfortable paying a subscription. Saving money shouldn't mean turning every simple service into another project.

Hardware upgrades became an endless rabbit hole

One upgrade always led to another

I initially thought my existing hardware would be enough to run most of my self-hosted services. But as I experimented with more applications, I started paying closer attention to my server's limitations. Some services needed more RAM, while others benefited from a faster processor or additional storage. Before long, I was considering upgrades I hadn't planned to buy.

The problem was that every upgrade opened the door to something else. More powerful hardware meant I could run heavier applications, which made me curious about trying even more services. I kept finding new reasons to improve my setup, even when my existing hardware was doing its job.

Looking back, I realized there was no clear finish line. I could always buy something better or build a more capable server. Instead of treating hardware as a one-time investment, I had turned it into an ongoing expense. The money saved on subscriptions didn't always stay saved.

6 self-hosted services that are just as useful on your phone as on your desktop

I rebuilt my self-hosted stack around apps that don't leave my phone behind.

By  Yash Patel

I still self-host, but saving money isn't my only goal anymore

I haven't given up on self-hosting, and I don't think you should either. I just look at it differently now. Instead of trying to replace every paid service, I focus on what genuinely benefits from running on my own hardware. For me, privacy, control, and the freedom to experiment can justify the extra cost. But I no longer assume that free software automatically means cheaper ownership. Sometimes, paying for a reliable service is the smarter choice. Self-hosting makes the most sense when I know why I'm doing it, not just because I can.

item.title: Your router avoids the best 5GHz channels by default, and turning on DFS gave my Wi-Fi room to breathe
item.itunes:title: Your router avoids the best 5GHz channels by default, and turning on DFS gave my Wi-Fi room to breathe
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you set up a high-end router in a suburban neighborhood or apartment building, you might find that your 5GHz network is choking on overlapping channels while half the spectrum sits completely dormant. Out of the box, most consumer routers restrict themselves to the lower non-DFS 5GHz channels to avoid regulatory fines or interference with weather radar and military frequencies. By leaving dynamic frequency selection disabled, you are voluntarily fighting for scraps in a crowded four-channel pool. Unlocking DFS channels opens up a massive interference-free superhighway that gives your Wi-Fi network room to breathe.

I finally made my Wi-Fi snappier by changing the most ignored setting on my router

Your router's transmit power isn't supposed to be at the maximum level

11
By  Tanveer Singh

DFS isn't illegal

But there are some regulations

What actually is DFS, or dynamic frequency selection? DFS channels sit right in frequency ranges shared with weather radar systems, satellite communications, and aviation Doppler radars. You're essentially sharing the spectrum with all of these.

It's not illegal to use these channels. You're not committing a crime by switching DFS on, but you must follow mandatory rules when using these channels.

To legally use DFS channels, FCC regulations require that your router or access point continuously monitor the frequency. If it then detects even a whisper of radar signatures, it must immediately vacate the channel and jump to a non-DFS frequency, causing a momentary disconnect as the AP shifts traffic. This momentary disconnect is essentially a fear of radar and the reason why so many manufacturers keep DFS turned off or buried in advanced settings by default.

However, unlocking gear is a major game changer for power users, giving you real-world advantages that make a big difference in day-to-day use. Four standard non-DFS channels are available, and every router in your apartment building or neighborhood is likely stacked on top of each other within them. By switching on DFS, you're escaping those lower-band bottlenecks, as it opens up a much wider, sparsely populated block of frequencies.

Because fewer consumer devices and neighbors operate on DFS channels, you can comfortably run wider channel configurations like 80 MHz or even a clean 160 MHz block without instantly colliding with co-channel interference.

Setting up DFS channels isn't hard

Use a Wi-Fi analyzer for more information

Before you start, complete an audit of your Wi-Fi and connection. You can do this by scanning your local RF environment. You can download a range of free Wi-Fi analyzer tools on your mobile phone. These will let you see how crowded the lower 5GHz channels are in your area compared to the quieter DFS range. Using your phone, you can move through your house and see how that shifts in different areas.

Once you've done this, you can then access your advanced router settings and navigate to the 5GHz wireless configuration page. This is where you can enable DFS channels by toggling on DFS channel support. You can select an open DFS channel or set your channel auto-selection to include DFS bands and then apply settings. Use the information you got from your Wi-Fi audit to choose the most suitable channel for yourself.

Once you've done this, monitor and verify. Check your client connection speeds, signal metrics, and stability to confirm your devices have successfully migrated to the new clean spectrum. Using your Wi-Fi analyzer tool again should show whether this change made a difference.

This might not work for everyone

Close to an airport? Think again

This change won't work for everyone. There can be some compatibility quirks. If you live near a major airport or a meteorological Doppler radar station, your router might occasionally drop a client for a few seconds as it automatically vacates the DFS channel when it detects radar pulses. If you don't live near devices that use this, it won't make much of a difference, but near airports, the constant dropping out can be frustrating, even if it's only for short periods.

Before switching, also confirm client device support. Many older smart home devices or niche client devices might not support DFS channels. Most modern smartphones, laptops, and streaming boxes do, but some legacy IoT chips can occasionally be picky.

Don't lose out on performance

Check if DFS channels are right for you

Consumer routers play it safe out of the box to avoid regulatory headaches, leaving half of the 5GHz spectrum gathering dust. Forcing your network to utilize DFS channels is one of the easiest ways to bypass neighborhood congestion. Log in to your router, toggle on DFS, and give your high-speed wireless devices the open highway they deserve.

item.title: The 16GB gaming PC is officially dead and current RAM pricing proves it
item.itunes:title: The 16GB gaming PC is officially dead and current RAM pricing proves it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, 16GB of RAM felt like the sweet spot for PC building, especially gaming PCs, because it let you keep Discord, a dozen Chrome tabs, and a background capture app open without breaking a sweat.

However, when you launch a modern 2026 title, like an Unreal Engine 5 heavy hitter or even a poorly optimized port, this instantly exposes the bottleneck despite your other specs. Your system memory usage spikes and background tasks get aggressive, and microstutters destroy your 1% low frame rates. The era of the 16GB gaming PC feels over. Driven by shifting Steam Hardware Survey trends, volatile memory pricing realities, and ballooning asset sizes, 32GB is no longer a luxury upgrade. It's instead the mandatory baseline for any serious build.

5 reasons DDR4 RAM is still good enough that you don't need to upgrade

DDR4 RAM might not be your first choice, but it still has a few advantages that make it relevant in 2024

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Steam hardware surveys tell a major story

And developers have stopped optimizing for 16GB

Industry telemetry and player hardware trends have changed dramatically over the past couple of years, as shown by the Steam hardware survey, which has historically been dominated by 16GB, but that dominance has slowly eroded as AAA developers abandoned last-gen console constraints. 32GB configurations have surged immensely in the monthly Steam hardware survey data, becoming almost the de facto standard amongst enthusiasts and mid- to high-end tier builders.

This is mostly because developers have stopped optimizing for 16GB altogether. With current-gen consoles packing unified memory pools and PC ports leaning heavily on massive uncompressed asset streaming, modern titles routinely chew through 12 to 14GB of system RAM alone. This is before you even account for the operating system, background daemons, or other applications you have open on the side.

For a lot of gamers, this might feel expensive, but realistically refusing to buy 32GB over cost savings makes zero sense in the current market. In most cases, but not all, buying a 32GB kit gives you a much better cost-per-gigabyte sweet spot. DDR5 pricing has stabilized somewhat after its early-adoption rollercoaster, making 2 × 16GB (32GB) kits a better value than lower-capacity alternatives. Buying a 16GB kit today will save you pennies while creating an instant bottleneck within your gaming PC, and when it comes to future upgrades too.

Trying to match or upgrade 16GB later by slapping two more sticks in can often force memory controllers into lower command rates or unstable subtimings, making a single 32GB kit (2 x 16GB) the only sensible starting point.

Testing the difference opened my eyes

For a second I thought 16GB was pulling through

I decided to actually put the hardware I had to the test, and it really showed where 16GB began to fall apart. There was a physical penalty of running lower RAM on high-end hardware. My PC features an Intel Core i5-13600K paired with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 4080 as well as 4TB of PCIe 4.0 NVMe storage. I tested it with a 16GB kit (two 8GB sticks) versus a 32GB kit (two 16GB sticks), both running at optimized XMP speeds.

For a lot of AAA titles, average frame rates looked pretty similar. At first, it made me think 16GB was much more powerful than I expected. However, the real story was in the 1% and 0.1% loads. My 16GB system suffered massive frame-time spikes as the engine hit memory walls and triggered disk paging, even though the RTX 4080 rendered frames at lightning speed. Even though the average frames looked great on paper, the titles I was playing constantly stuttered, lagged, and froze. I noticed particularly large dips during rapid traversal or other fast-paced movement on screen.

Alongside this, I also felt like I had a major alt-tab penalty, to the point where I dreaded alt-tabbing out of a game when running on 16GB of RAM. With my normal setup, which features a 32GB kit, my system would recover pretty quickly when alt-tabbing and switching out of a memory-heavy game to something like Discord or a browser. However, with 16GB, my system stalled pretty significantly as cache is dumped.

Opt for 32GB moving forward

It does more than just prevent bottlenecks

When you're buying a new PC or configuring your next build, it's important to opt for a 32GB kit if you want a future-proofed machine. Realistically, you're better off skipping the 16GB kit entirely. Strike 16GB of RAM off of your parts list permanently and treat 32GB in the form of two 16GB dual-channel DDR5 as your non-negotiable floor for any mid- to high-end PC build moving forward.

Alongside RAM capacity, prioritize speed and latency. Sweet-spot memory speeds like DDR5-6000 CL30 will ensure that your memory bandwidth matches your CPU's memory controller constraints as well.

By choosing this amount of RAM and these higher speeds, you give your PC room to breathe. You keep your memory channels clean, avoid mixed-kit headaches, and build a system that won't need a RAM overhaul just 12 months down the line.

Don't cheap out on your memory

You'll risk bottlenecking your system

Saving $30 on a 16GB kit when you're already dropping a lot of cash on solid specs for the rest of your PC, like an RTX 4080 or a 13th gen processor, can feel like a false economy. When your frame times tank because your system is choking on swap files, that tiny upfront savings turns into a frustrating and pretty laggy gaming experience. Stop treating 16GB as acceptable for a modern gaming rig. Buy a 32GB kit, lock in your timings, and build a PC that actually unleashes your hardware.

Saving $30 on a 16GB kit when you're already dropping a lot of cash on solid specs for the rest of your PC, like an RTX 4080 or a 13th gen processor, can feel like a false economy. When your frame times tank because your system is choking on swap files, that tiny upfront savings turns into a frustrating and pretty laggy gaming experience. Stop treating 16GB as acceptable for a modern gaming rig. Buy a 32GB kit, lock in your timings, and build a PC that actually unleashes your hardware.
